## 1.2 Objects, vectors and missing values

### Save and calculate

- `<-` saves a value; R distinguishes uppercase from lowercase.
- Quoted text is character data. `TRUE` and `FALSE` are logical values.
- The following values are **illustrative planning inputs**, not extra Superstore records.

```{r}
unit_price <- 25
units <- 4
sales_value <- unit_price * units
sales_value
business_question <- "Which categories generate profit?"
sales_value > 80
```

### Work with several values

```{r}
# Illustrative order values, in dollars.
order_values <- c(25, 60, 100, 250)
mean(order_values)
median(order_values)
order_values[1]                    # R starts counting at 1
order_values[order_values >= 100]   # Keep entries meeting a condition
```

- `==`: equals; `!=`: differs; `&`: AND; `|`: OR; `%in%`: belongs to a set.
- `NA` means missing. It is different from zero.
- Check why a value is missing before excluding it.

```{r}
values_with_missing <- c(25, 60, NA, 250)
is.na(values_with_missing)
mean(values_with_missing)                 # Missingness propagates
mean(values_with_missing, na.rm = TRUE)   # Mean of the observed values only
sum(is.na(values_with_missing))
```

## 1.3 Import the retail data

- [Download the order-line CSV](../data/business/superstore-lines.csv).
- One row is **one product line within an order**.
- One order can have several lines. One customer can place several orders.
- Use the supplied CSV so your results match the course's pinned version.

```{r}
#| label: r-intro-import
# This cell works from the project root or the lessons/ folder.
data_dir <- if (dir.exists("data")) "data" else file.path("..", "data")
source(file.path(data_dir, "..", "lessons", "_includes", "course-tools.R"))
lines <- read.csv(file.path(data_dir, "business", "superstore-lines.csv"),
                  stringsAsFactors = FALSE, colClasses = c(postal_code = "character"))
orders <- make_orders(lines)
c(order_lines = nrow(lines), orders = nrow(orders),
  customers = n_distinct(lines$customer_id))
```

- `read.csv()` creates a **data frame**: variables in columns, records in rows.
- `source()` loads the shared chart style and the explained order-summary function.
- `make_orders()` checks agreement of order attributes and sums sales, profit and units within each order.
- It calculates shipping time from order date to ship date; this is **not delivery time**.

```{r}
names(lines)
str(lines[c("order_id", "category", "sales", "quantity", "discount", "profit")])
knitr::kable(head(lines[c("order_id", "category", "sales", "profit")]), digits = 2)
colSums(is.na(lines))
```

- Postal codes and IDs are labels, even when they contain digits.
- `discount = 0.20` means 20%, not 0.20%.
- Negative profit is a recorded loss, not automatically a data error.
- This extract has no missing cells; other datasets may do so.

## 1.4 Select, filter and create variables

- `select()` chooses columns.
- `filter()` chooses rows.
- `mutate()` adds or transforms variables.
- `%>%` passes the result of one step to the next.

```{r}
loss_lines <- lines %>%
  filter(profit < 0) %>%
  select(order_id, category, sub_category, sales, discount, profit)
knitr::kable(head(loss_lines), digits = 2)

line_flags <- lines %>%
  mutate(loss_line = profit < 0,
         discount_pct = 100 * discount)
c(loss_lines = sum(line_flags$loss_line),
  loss_line_pct = 100 * mean(line_flags$loss_line))
```

- The denominator above is **6,682 order lines**.
- A loss-making line does not necessarily make the whole order unprofitable.

## 1.5 Group and summarize

```{r}
category_summary <- lines %>%
  group_by(category) %>%
  summarise(line_count = n(),
            total_sales = sum(sales),
            total_profit = sum(profit),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(margin_pct = 100 * total_profit / total_sales) %>%
  arrange(desc(total_profit))
knitr::kable(category_summary, digits = 2)
```

- `group_by()` defines which records belong together.
- `summarise()` returns one row per group.
- Overall margin is **total profit / total sales**.
- Averaging individual line margins gives a different, equally weighted statistic.

## 1.6 Make and interpret a chart

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart: Technology and Office Supplies contribute much more recorded profit than Furniture."
#| label: intro-category-profit
#| fig-cap: "Recorded profit by category, US Superstore orders placed in 2023–2025."
ggplot(category_summary, aes(x = reorder(category, total_profit), y = total_profit)) +
  geom_col(fill = petra_ink) + coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Recorded profit ($)")
```

- Furniture contributes much less profit than the other two categories in this extract.
- Compare its margin and subcategories before proposing an action.
- A chart identifies a pattern; it does not establish why the pattern occurred.
